explain: C++ starts from C: types, statements with ;, blocks { } and functions are the same. It adds new tools on top.
remember: C++ = C plus more (++ means "one more").

explain: Namespaces and ::  std::string means "string from the std library". :: reads as "inside".
Classes: a type with data and functions (methods) together. Use a dot to reach them.
References: int &n is another name for the same variable, so the function can change it. Like a pointer without the *.
remember: & in a type = "the same one, not a copy".

explain: Templates: <T> is a type left blank, filled in when you use it. One function for many types.
std::vector<int> is a namespace (std::), a template (<int>) and a class with methods (.push_back) all at once.
remember: Read it piece by piece: where :: what <type> . do

explain: cout << is an operator that a class defines. << sends each value into the output stream, one after another.
remember: Arrows point where the data flows: into cout.

explain: std::cout prints. << sends values to it. std::endl ends the line.
example: The start of every C++ program.

explain: std::string is text that grows by itself. += adds to it, size() counts letters.
std::vector is a list that grows. push_back adds to the end. for (int n : nums) goes through it.
example: A list of scores, players, or files.

explain: int& is a reference: another name for the same variable, so the function changes the original.
example: Updating a big object without copying it.

explain: A class bundles data and functions. public parts can be used outside; private parts cannot.
A template writes one function that works for many types (T).
example: Containers and helpers that work with any data, like std::vector itself.

explain: std::map stores values under keys, kept in sorted order. auto lets the compiler work out the type.
example: Counting words, or looking up a user by name.

syntax:
std::cout << "Sum: " << 2 + 3 << "\n";
std::cerr << "Something went wrong\n";
explain: cout prints, cerr prints errors. << sends each piece in order.
cin >> reads one word or number. getline reads the whole line.
using namespace std lets you skip std::. auto lets the compiler pick the type.
Range-for goes through every item. The classic for counts.
const auto& reads each item without copying it.
example: Fast loops over big strings or objects.

syntax:
std::string s = "hello world";
std::cout << s.size() << " " << s.substr(0, 5) << " " << s.find("world") << "\n";
explain: size, substr(start, length), find (gives std::string::npos if not found).
+= joins text. stoi turns text into int, to_string turns numbers into text.
push_back adds to the end, pop_back removes, at() checks the index is safe.
sort and reverse work on a range: from begin() to end().
find gives an iterator; end() means "not found". max_element finds the biggest.

syntax:
#include <numeric>
int total = std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0);
explain: accumulate adds up everything, starting from 0.
Give sort a lambda to choose how to compare.
example: Sorting by age, price, or name.

explain: [] is the capture list: which outside variables the lambda can use.
example: Small helper functions inside other functions.

syntax:
std::array<int, 3> a = {1, 2, 3};
std::cout << a.size();
explain: std::array is a fixed-size array that knows its size.
[name, age] unpacks each pair. count says if a key exists.
unordered_map is faster than map but not sorted. [] makes the key if missing.
set keeps unique values, sorted.

syntax:
std::pair<std::string, int> p = {"Ada", 36};
std::cout << p.first << " " << p.second;
explain: pair holds two values together.
example: Returning two things from a function.

explain: : x(x), y(y) is an initializer list. const after a method means it doesn't change the object.
A struct is a class where everything is public. Good for plain data.
static belongs to the class, shared by all objects.
= 0 makes a pure virtual (must be written by children). override checks you really replace one.
example: Many shapes, one way to use them.

explain: The destructor ~Name runs by itself when the object goes away.
example: Closing files and freeing memory automatically.

explain: new makes memory by hand, delete gives it back. Prefer smart pointers.
example: Old-style code you'll see in tutorials.

explain: Smart pointers free memory by themselves. unique_ptr has one owner, shared_ptr many.
A class template works for any type T.
example: Containers like vector are made this way.

explain: Operator overloading makes + work for your own types.
throw sends an error, catch handles it. what() gives the message.
example: Handling bad input or missing files.

explain: optional may or may not hold a value. value_or gives a fallback.
enum class keeps names inside the enum: Color::Red.
A namespace groups names so they don't clash with others.
A reference is another name for the same variable.
example: Changing a variable inside a function.

explain: ofstream writes a file, ifstream reads one.
stringstream reads numbers and words out of a string.

syntax:
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o main main.cpp
./main
g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp utils.cpp -o app
explain: -std=c++17 picks the C++ version, -Wall shows warnings.
#pragma once stops a header being included twice. "" includes your own files.
